sentences.text: He found the cache in the June and it took him two months and a great deal of walking, and the method was not sophisticated: he watched, and he wrote down the direction, and he did that eleven times over eight weeks.
Watching is most of it and watching is dull.

He sat on the wall by the byre with a book he was not reading for something in the region of forty hours across that spring, and he saw a fox six times, and only three of those were carrying anything.
The other five directions came from his mother and from the Hansdóttir boy, who both agreed to tell him and who both, he is fairly sure, thought he was wasting a summer.
Everything went north-east.

The cache is under a slab on the seaward side of the ridge, about two kilometres from the last house, in a place with no particular features that Ari has ever been able to describe to anybody without drawing a map.
He got the slab up with a fence post and he sat back on his heels and looked at it for a long time.
There were, by his count that afternoon, ninety-four items.
He counted them twice, out on the grass, in two rows, and then put every single one back before he left, which took the better part of an hour and which he has always been glad about.
Gloves: forty-one, not one of them a pair.
Socks: nineteen.
Four hats.
The boot lining.
A great deal of raw sheep's wool of the kind that comes off a fence in June and that nobody would ever miss.

Two lengths of knitting still on the needles, which he took home and which turned out to have gone from a windowsill in 2021 and which caused, when he produced them, the largest reaction of the entire summer.
And the sheepskin, folded, at the back, four kilos of it, dragged two kilometres uphill by an animal that weighs three and a half.
It was dry.
That is the thing that undid him.
It is under a slab on a seaward ridge in Iceland and there is drainage under it that Ari has never been able to work out, and the whole of it was dry and none of it was chewed.
Nothing had been eaten.
Nothing had been shredded for bedding.
It was not a nest — there was no den within sixty metres and he checked properly, with a torch, over two visits.
It was a store, and it had been sorted.
He has been back perhaps sixty times since and the number goes up and down.
The highest he has counted is a hundred and forty-one, in the September he was seventeen.
The lowest was thirty-eight, one April, after a winter that everybody on that coast remembers.
That April is the only real evidence he has that any of it is for anything.
Fifty-odd items of wool went out of that cache between October and March and none of it was in the ditches and none of it came home.

The wool was at the back and the manufactured things were at the front and the four hats were together, and Ari has never once been able to decide whether that last observation is real or whether he is a person who found ninety-four objects under a rock and wanted them to mean something.
